# Sources ledger: the human body (topic discovery)

Five sources were read (S1-S5). The rest are search summaries kept as leads: nothing in the chosen film rests on them,
and each says what it would be needed for.

### S1. William E. Brownell, "What Is Electromotility? The History of Its Discovery and Its Relevance to Acoustics", Acoustics Today (Acoustical Society of America) 13(1):20-27, Spring 2017
- Secondary: a historical account by the scientist whose team discovered outer-hair-cell electromotility (author manuscript on PubMed Central, PMC5645053). URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5645053/
- Access: read (the author manuscript's history sections on Gold, Kemp, electromotility, prestin and the prestin knockout, through a page reader that quoted them; figures and the supplementary video not seen)
- Supports: C01, C03, C04, C06, C08, C10, C11, C13, C17. Counterevidence: dates Kemp's first report to 1978 where S2 says 1979; it does not mention Gold's warning that the ear could ring (S2 does). It is written by a protagonist of the outer-hair-cell story, so its weight on the cell body as the energy source is set against S2, which calls the oscillator's origin unclear; it says itself that prestin's precise role "remain[s] to be identified" and that the outer hair cell's contribution is known "with reasonable certainty".
- Status: credible secondary (expert author, 2017); nothing found replaces it; independent of S2.

### S2. Thomas Duke, "The power of hearing", Physics World (IOP Publishing), 2 May 2002
- Popular: a feature by a Royal Society University Research Fellow at the Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, who worked on the physics of hearing. URL: https://physicsworld.com/a/the-power-of-hearing
- Access: read (the whole feature, through a page reader that quoted it)
- Supports: C01, C02, C03, C05, C06, C07, C08, C09, C11, C12, C14, C17. Counterevidence: dates Kemp's finding to 1979 (S1: 1978). It is 24 years old: newer structural work on prestin (2022-2023, seen only in search summaries) studies how the motor moves; nothing found overturns this account. It states openly that the oscillator's origin was unclear and that spontaneous oscillation of an outer hair cell had never been observed.
- Status: credible popular account by a specialist; independent of S1.

### S3. C. Mo, B. McPherson, T.-F. Ma, "Cochlear Function in Individuals with and without Spontaneous Otoacoustic Emissions", Audiology Research 13(5):686-699 (MDPI), 2023
- Primary: an original study of 463 normal-hearing adults aged 20-59 (Han Chinese university staff and students, convenience sampling); refereed, per its acknowledgements. URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10514821/ (doi:10.3390/audiolres13050060)
- Access: read (introduction, methods, discussion and limitations, through a page reader; the prevalence figure and the supplementary table were not in the text read)
- Supports: C16. Counterevidence: none found on the clinical use. Its conclusion is hedged ("appear to be a useful marker of cochlear health"), its sample is narrow, and its prevalence data were not seen, so it supports no number here.
- Status: primary record, used only for how otoacoustic emissions are used.

### S4. Patricia M. White (principal investigator), White Lab research page "Regeneration After Noise Induced Hearing Loss", University of Rochester Medical Center, undated (seen 2026-11-24)
- Secondary: a hearing-regeneration lab's own summary of its field. URL: https://www.urmc.rochester.edu/labs/white-lab.aspx
- Access: read (the whole page)
- Supports: C15. Counterevidence: none found; unread leads agree (S15, and a University of Washington release seen in a search summary). The page does not say which hair cells noise harms first, so nothing here says outer hair cells are the most vulnerable.
- Status: credible but brief and undated; the only read source for C15, so likely.

### S5. Mark S. Anderson, Emily S. Venanzi, Ludger Klein, et al. (with Christophe Benoist and Diane Mathis), "Projection of an Immunological Self Shadow Within the Thymus by the Aire Protein", Science 298:1395-1401, 15 November 2002
- Primary: the study itself (peer-reviewed); PDF from the authors' lab site, doi:10.1126/science.1077464. URL: https://cbdm.hms.harvard.edu/assets/Publications/2002pub/AndersonScience%20II.pdf
- Access: read (abstract, introduction, the APECED passage and the discussion, from text extracted from the PDF; figures not seen)
- Supports: candidate T2's material (sources stand in for claims; T2 was not chosen). Counterevidence: the paper notes that an earlier study of aire-deficient mice blamed peripheral lymphocyte homeostasis instead; not all ectopic transcripts depend on aire; how aire controls several hundred genes was open.
- Status: primary record (2002); later work extends it (not read).

### S6. Nature Reviews Immunology, review on thymic medullary epithelial cells and negative selection (title and authors not seen)
- Secondary (review). URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/nri2450
- Access: snippet (search summary only)
- Supports: nothing on its own; a lead that the tissue-specific antigens of medullary epithelial cells are central to negative selection (T2). Counterevidence: not looked for.
- Status: lead, not read.

### S7. J. Haseleu et al., "Water-induced finger wrinkles do not affect touch acuity or dexterity in handling wet objects", PLoS One, 2014
- Primary: a 40-person study. URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24416318/ (full text: https://edoc.mdc-berlin.de/id/eprint/13817/1/13817oa.pdf)
- Access: snippet (search summary of the abstract, and of the full text's statement that it tested a hypothesis of Changizi et al.)
- Supports: T3 M3 (lead). Counterevidence: the hypothesis it tested; the search did not surface any test in that hypothesis's favour.
- Status: lead, not read.

### S8. Authors not seen, "Water immersion and EMLA cause similar digit skin wrinkling and vasoconstriction", 2003 (PubMed 12826076)
- Primary. URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12826076/
- Access: snippet (search summary only)
- Supports: T3 M1 (lead). Counterevidence: S11 disputes the nerve-signal account.
- Status: lead, not read.

### S9. E. P. V. Wilder-Smith (as the search summary attributes it), review on water-immersion wrinkling and vasoconstriction, Springer, about 2004 (year read from the DOI)
- Secondary (review). URL: https://link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s10286-004-0172-4
- Access: snippet (search summary only)
- Supports: T3 M1 (lead). Counterevidence: S11.
- Status: lead, not read.

### S10. Authors not seen, "Paradoxical response to water immersion in replanted fingers", 2006 (library record and publisher page)
- Primary. URL: https://vufind.lboro.ac.uk/PrimoRecord/cdi_proquest_miscellaneous_20735968 ; https://www.springermedizin.de/paradoxical-response-to-water-immersion-in-replanted-fingers/8780024
- Access: snippet (search summary only)
- Supports: T3 M2 (lead). Counterevidence: not looked for.
- Status: lead, not read.

### S11. Marasakatla and Marasakatla, PeerJ Preprints 57 (versions 3 and 4), date not seen
- Preprint, not peer-reviewed. URL: https://peerj.com/preprints/57v4.pdf
- Access: snippet (search summary only)
- Supports: T3 M4 (lead: a challenge to the nerve-signal explanation). Counterevidence: S8, S9, S10.
- Status: lead, not read; a minority view.

### S12. Hearing Health Matters (Hearing International blog), "The Von Bekesy - Gold Controversy", 2014
- Popular (blog). URL: https://hearinghealthmatters.org/hearing-international/2014/von-bekesy-thomas-gold-controversy/
- Access: snippet (search summary only)
- Supports: nothing used. Lead: Gold proposed that a microphone at the ear might pick up the ear's ring, and the attempt failed because 1948 microphones were not sensitive enough; also a Bekesy-Gold controversy (compare C04).
- Status: lead; to be read, with Gold's 1948 paper or his own later account, before any line tells the failed attempt.

### S13. R. C. Bilger et al., 1990, prevalence of spontaneous otoacoustic emissions in 131 normal-hearing people (title not seen)
- Primary. URL: https://scilit.com/publications/bd61409cd0bedc4727059c2dcbdc3e92
- Access: snippet (search summary only)
- Supports: nothing used. Lead: estimated prevalence 0.533 in women and 0.268 in men; another unread summary gives "about 40%" of normal-hearing people.
- Status: lead; no prevalence number goes in the film until a source for it is read.

### S14. M. C. Liberman et al., Nature, 2002, prestin-deficient mice (doi:10.1038/nature01059; title not seen)
- Primary. URL: https://www.doi.org/10.1038/NATURE01059
- Access: snippet (the search summary quoted its abstract)
- Supports: nothing on its own; C13 rests on S1. Lead: "a 40-60 dB loss of cochlear sensitivity in vivo, with mechanotransduction intact".
- Status: lead; read the abstract before any line gives a number.

### S15. Stanford Institute for Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine, news article "A new understanding of how birds regenerate hearing may lead to therapies for people with hearing loss", undated
- Popular (institutional news). URL: https://med.stanford.edu/stemcell/news/iscbrmarticles/hearing-regeneration.html
- Access: snippet (search summary only)
- Supports: nothing on its own; agrees with C15 (birds restore lost cochlear hair cells; no therapy yet does this in people).
- Status: lead, not read.
